What we make

Three ways to keep it.

More than a keepsake — an experience to treasure.

Each one includes two files: your heartbeat or voice, optimized for quality, and one with gentle music for an atmosphere of remembering.

The HeartSong Portrait

A heartbeat set to music, on a frame you can hang or place somewhere special.

$285

The face you love, and beside it a recording to treasure — on a small drive, so it doesn't get lost in your email. Play it through a Bluetooth speaker rather than a phone and you'll feel the beat as it plays. The two Bluetooth speakers we recommend are below.

Send any 5×7 photo you love.
Or, if you can, photograph the recording itself — a hand on a chest, the two of you in that room.

The Ever-There Bear

Their picture on the front, their heartbeat or voice inside.

$285

Send us a heartbeat, or send us their catchphrases — recorded with our equipment or straight off your phone. We clean it up and tuck it into a sound box inside a bear. Press it, and there they are.

A frame on the front holds a photograph you send us, so the face and the sound end up in the same pair of hands.

Takes replaceable batteries on purpose, so it can be revived in ten years. Removable pouch — the bear is washable, the module isn't.

The Held Heart

A smooth, solid heart that plays when you press it.

$285

The smallest of the three and the easiest to carry — smooth and solid rather than soft, about the width of your palm. It sits on a nightstand or goes in a bag. Press the heart and it plays; press it again and it stops. Nothing to plug in, nothing to figure out.

Good for children, for hospital rooms, and for anyone who would rather hold something than open a file. The shell wipes clean.

Two ways to get us the sound.

The price above is the whole thing, whichever keepsake you choose. The only thing that changes it is how the recording reaches us.

What we recommend

We send you the recording kit

$285  everything included

A recorder and a stethoscope microphone arrive at your door — usually within the week once it ships — with the postage already paid both ways and a card showing you exactly what to do. Using our equipment is the difference between a recording you'll want to listen to and one that sounds thin.

$100 of that price is the equipment and the round-trip postage. Because we only have a few kits, we'll tell you the current wait before you pay.

If you already have a recording

You send us your own

$185  $100 less

Already have a recording — from a hospital monitor, a voice you saved, a file someone made for you? Send it and we'll work from that. No kit, no postage, and $100 off.

One honest word: we don't recommend trying to record a heartbeat without proper equipment. A heartbeat sits at the very bottom of what a microphone can hear, and a phone held to a chest usually doesn't reach it. For voices, a phone is fine.

Pets are welcome on all three. Dogs and cats have hearts too!

How it works

Five steps, and we walk you through every one.

1

Choose your keepsake

The frame, the bear, or the heart. Tell us what you’d like and how to reach you.

We’ll write back with a PayPal link or a Venmo request, and a timeline — when the recording kit will reach you, and our best estimate of when you’ll receive the keepsake.

2

Capture the sound in a moment that means something

We mail you a recording kit with the postage already paid, both ways, and a card that shows you exactly how to do the recording.

In the Philadelphia area it may be possible for us to come and do it in person.

3

Send it back

Email the recording to studio@legacyheartsongs.com using the instructions in the kit, then drop the kit in the prepaid envelope.

Emailing the sound file is the surest way to get it safely into our hands. That said, if saving and sending files isn't your thing, just send back the kit and we'll do it for you.

4

A musician goes to work

We clean the recording up until it sounds right, then music is layered around it and arranged so the heartbeat stays the hero.

5

It arrives

A few minutes of music, in your inbox and in your hands. Something to play at a birthday, an anniversary, or on a quiet afternoon, for as many years as you want it.

The process takes about three to four weeks, start to finish. We have a limited number of kits, so we'll tell you the current wait before you pay.

Our musicians

Every note is played by one of us — three generations of us.

Nothing here is generated. We don't use AI for music composition. Sometimes the strings are a keyboard — but a person is playing them, one note at a time. And a person listens to every piece before it leaves.

Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

For our detail people.

If your question isn't answered, write to us and we'll get back to you.

What does it cost?

$285 — the same for the Portrait, the Bear and the Heart. That covers the recording kit mailed to your door, the postage both ways, the engineering, the music, both audio files, and your keepsake.

$185 if you already have a recording and send it to us yourself. No kit goes out, so we take $100 off. That $100 covers the equipment — its wear, loss and replacement — and the round-trip postage. That's the whole difference between the two.

How do I pay?

Tell us what you'd like on the start-the-process page. We'll write back within one business day with the current wait for a kit, and a PayPal link — or a Venmo request instead, if you'd rather.

We ask for the whole amount at the start rather than chasing you for a balance later. We'd rather the last thing you hear from us be the music.

Nothing is charged until you've seen the wait time and said yes.

What if I need to cancel?

Before the kit goes in the mail, we refund everything, no questions and no awkwardness.

Once the kit has been mailed, we refund everything except the $100 that covers the equipment and the postage, as soon as the kit is back with us. Send it back in the prepaid envelope and we'll take care of the rest.

What's in the recording kit — and why is there sometimes a wait?

It isn't an ordinary stethoscope. Ours is customized so you can listen and record at the same time. The microphone inside is specialized too: its range reaches down into the low frequencies where a heartbeat actually lives, which most microphones miss. And the recorder has a quality preamp built in, so what it captures is clean from the start.

All of that means a single kit costs us nearly as much as a whole order. We keep a small number in circulation, which is why you may sometimes wait for one — and why we always tell you how long before you pay.

Did you change my person's heartbeat?

A little, and here's exactly what we did.

Most hearts don't land on a musical tempo. Yours was probably a few beats off from the song you chose, so we nudged the speed — usually by a few percent — until the two agreed.

We also cleaned the recording up: took out the rumble underneath, along with the sounds of clothing and movement. Then we looped the steadiest passages we could find, so the beat holds even and unbroken all the way through the song.

What we didn't do is replace anything or generate anything, so the sound you sent is the sound that gets sent back. The second file we send you is the heartbeat at its exact original speed, so you have that too.

Is any of this made by AI?

No. Every note is performed by one of us, in real time. Sometimes a flute or a string section is a keyboard patch — but a person is playing it, making choices about timing and touch.

How do I make a good recording?

The card in the kit walks you through it, but here is the whole of it:

  • Make three separate recordings, about thirty seconds each.
  • Go to the quietest room you can, or make the room as quiet as possible. Turn off the dishwasher and the television. Listen for the refrigerator — it's a low hum you stop noticing, and you can unplug it for a few minutes (don't forget to plug it back in!). Listen for traffic and for dogs.
  • Ask your person to breathe evenly and as quietly as they can.
  • Hold the stethoscope still. Light pressure, not firm (which is the opposite of what everyone expects).

Once the three recordings are saved, and if you can, move the files to a computer with the USB cord in the kit and email them to us. That gets us working sooner and means the recordings won't get lost in the mail. You may need to send one file per email, since they're large. And if transferring files isn't your thing, say so — we'll pull them off the recorder when the kit comes back, and it's no trouble at all.

What if the recording doesn't come out?

Write to studio@legacyheartsongs.com and we'll fix it. If there's still time, we'll send a second kit at no charge. If there isn't — and sometimes there isn't — we'll talk it through with you honestly and find the right thing to do, which may be a refund.

Some chests are harder to record than others, and it isn't your fault when one is. If you tell us up front who we're recording, we can often steer you to the setup most likely to work the first time.

What exactly arrives, and on what?

Two audio files, always: the song, and the heartbeat on its own at its true speed.

They come to your inbox, and they come on a small drive that lives with your keepsake — so the sound isn't stranded in an email you have to go looking for.

Even so: please save a copy somewhere else. Email it to yourself, put it in a cloud folder, give a copy to one other person in the family. Drives fail, and this is the one file you can't remake.

How should I listen to it?

On a Bluetooth speaker or a stereo, not a phone. The difference is not subtle — a heartbeat lives at the very bottom of what a speaker can reproduce, and a phone speaker simply cannot get down there.

Hold the speaker in your hands while it plays, if you can. You'll feel the beat as well as hear it, and that turns out to be the part people remember.

Can I record a baby, or a pet?

Pets, absolutely, and we won't treat it as a lesser request.

Babies and animals have much faster hearts, so rather than dragging the music up to meet them, we usually let the beat fall on the off-beats — it sits inside the groove instead of fighting it. It sounds right, and it's still exactly their heart.

One thing we don't do: fetal heartbeats recorded on a home doppler. That's a different legal world and we stay out of it.

Can I share it, or post it?

Share it with your family as much as you like — send it to every cousin, play it at the service, put it on a phone for someone who can't travel.

What we ask is that it isn't broadcast as open media — not posted publicly, not used in a video for an audience. That's a copyright matter on the music underneath it, and it protects you as much as us. If you want something you can post publicly, tell us and we'll build it that way from the start.

Is this medical in any way?

No, and we want to be very clear about it. A heart song is a keepsake. It is not a medical device, it doesn't detect or diagnose anything, and nothing about how it sounds tells you anything about anyone's health. Please don't read it that way, and please talk to a doctor about anything medical.

Can I talk to an actual person first?

Yes, and we'd rather you did. Write to info@legacyheartsongs.com and tell us as much or as little as you want. We answer every email ourselves, usually the same day.

There is no deadline on our end, no hold on a kit that expires, and nobody will follow up to pressure you. If you write once and then don't write again for six months, that's completely fine.

More is coming here: printable instruction sheets for the recording kit, and short videos showing how to get a clean recording with the equipment in the bag.

While they're still here to hear it.

The best time to record a heartbeat is an ordinary afternoon, with nothing wrong. If that's where you are, start there.
